title: Teaching by the Spirit
focus: Practice topic: opening a lesson and listening
intro: Only the Holy Ghost can bring true conversion. A missionary can open the way. In this lesson learners study how the Spirit helps those who teach and those who learn, and how to invite Him by how they begin, teach, listen and act.
preparation: Study Doctrine and Covenants 42:14 and Doctrine and Covenants 50:13–14, 17–23. Study Luke 12:12, John 14:26, 1 Nephi 2:16, 2 Nephi 33:1, Alma 18:16, Moroni 10:5 and Doctrine and Covenants 6:14–15, 23. Pray for each learner by name.

sections.title: Teaching by the Spirit
paras: Tell of President Brigham Young’s conversion, when the simple testimony of a humble man reached his heart. Ask: What does his experience teach about teaching by the Spirit? Help learners see that we must be sincere, speak from the heart and be humble (see Doctrine and Covenants 136:33).

Read Doctrine and Covenants 42:14 and Doctrine and Covenants 50:13–14, 17–23. The Lord has commanded that the gospel be taught by the Spirit. Ask what happens, according to Doctrine and Covenants 50:22, when a missionary teaches by the Spirit: both understand one another and rejoice together.

The Spirit is not always shown by tears. Read President Howard W. Hunter’s caution: strong emotion should not be confused with the Spirit itself, who brings “a great manifestation of the truth, of revelation to the heart.”

sections.title: How the Spirit helps teachers and learners
paras: Write these references on the board and let pairs study them: Luke 12:12 (He teaches what to say), John 14:26 (He brings things to remembrance), 1 Nephi 2:16 (He softens hearts), 2 Nephi 33:1 (He carries truth to the heart), Alma 18:16 (He helps us discern thoughts), Moroni 10:5 (He witnesses of truth) and Doctrine and Covenants 6:14–15, 23 (He enlightens the mind and gives peace).
One partner looks for how the Spirit helps the teacher, the other for how He helps the learner. Then they compare. Ask why this matters for a missionary.

sections.title: Inviting the Spirit as you teach
paras: Four skills help: begin a lesson in a way that invites the Spirit, adjust your teaching to the needs of the person, teach for understanding, and listen. Let four groups each take one skill and say how it invites the Spirit.
Ask: How does keeping a message simple help the Spirit teach? How does listening help? Let learners write how they will use these skills.

sections.title: Helping others recognize the Spirit
paras: Conversion needs the investigator to feel the Spirit work within him or her. Ask: How can you tell when someone feels the Holy Ghost? Elder M. Russell Ballard taught, “Experiences with the Spirit follow naturally when a person is willing to experiment upon the word” (“Now Is the Time,” Ensign, November 2000).
Read Doctrine and Covenants 11:12 in pairs. Ask how it would help if someone asked what the Holy Ghost feels like.

sections.title: Acting on the Spirit
paras: Read this from Elder Richard G. Scott, “How to Obtain Revelation and Inspiration for Your Personal Life,” Ensign, May 2012: “We receive help from our Father in Heaven in response to our faith, obedience, and the proper use of agency.”

President Boyd K. Packer taught that the Spirit whispers and does not shout (“The Candle of the Lord,” Ensign, January 1983). Ask what makes it hard to hear a whisper today, and what humility has to do with it (see 1 Corinthians 2:11, 14 and Moroni 7:13).
Study how the Spirit guided two missionaries: Peter in Acts 4:5–13 and Paul in Acts 16:6–15. Ask how each used agency to follow the Spirit, and what followed.

steps.why: Teach the idea and why it matters for a missionary.

examples.title: Name the four skills
examples.text: Write four words on the board: begin, adjust, understand, listen. Say how each one makes room for the Spirit.

examples.title: Show the Spirit’s work
examples.text: Use Luke 12:12 and John 14:26 to show how the Spirit helps a teacher, and 1 Nephi 2:16 to show how He helps a learner.

examples.title: Explain the whisper
examples.text: Read what President Packer taught about the whisper of the Spirit. Ask why a quiet, undistracted setting helps.

steps.why: Show one example of what learners will do.

examples.title: Open a lesson well
examples.text: Show a warm opening: a greeting, a short prayer, a simple question about the person’s life and a clear purpose.

examples.title: Show real listening
examples.text: Ask one question, then listen fully. Repeat back what you heard and answer what matters to the person.

examples.title: Show how to help someone feel the Spirit
examples.text: Use Doctrine and Covenants 11:12 to describe what the Spirit may feel like, then invite the person to share what they feel.

steps.why: Learners practise in pairs or small groups.

examples.title: Open and listen in pairs
examples.text: One learner opens a short lesson, asks one question and listens. The other plays an investigator. Switch.

examples.title: Teach in threes
examples.text: A missionary, an investigator and an observer. The observer watches for signs that the Spirit is present.

examples.title: Plan a simple message
examples.text: Each learner writes one short gospel message for a person they know, with one question to listen to.

steps.why: Name what went well and what can improve.

examples.title: Partner feedback
examples.text: The learner who was taught says what was clearest and what felt most sincere. The teacher writes one thing to keep and one to improve.

examples.title: Three questions
examples.text: Ask: What went well? What would you change? What helped the listener most to understand how to teach by the Spirit? Begin with the good.

examples.title: Simple checklist
examples.text: Was it simple? Was a scripture used and explained? Was the listener invited to act? Did the teacher speak with sincerity?

steps.why: Practise again with what was learned.

examples.title: Switch roles
examples.text: The learner who listened now teaches. Leave time for feedback both ways, then ask a few to share what they learned.

examples.title: Improve one thing
examples.text: Each learner teaches again and changes one thing from the feedback: a clearer sentence, a better scripture or a warmer invitation.

examples.title: Teach a new partner
examples.text: Find a new partner. Teach the same lesson again in a few minutes. Share one insight with the class.

testimony: Invite learners to share how the Lord has blessed them through His Spirit. Testify that as they seek Him, their ability to teach by the Spirit will grow.

tips.text: Give learners something to look for before a video, a quote or a passage.
Work in pairs so everyone can speak and listen safely.
Invite learners to testify by asking what they have felt and learned.
Remind learners that the Spirit is not always shown by tears.

quote.text: The Spirit does not get our attention by shouting or shaking us with a heavy hand. Rather it whispers.
quote.by: President Boyd K. Packer, “The Candle of the Lord,” Ensign, January 1983

study: Read Doctrine and Covenants 50:22 together and ask what happens when teacher and learner both feel the Spirit.
invitations: Watch some episodes of The District on the Church’s website as you prepare to serve.
Practise different ways to begin a lesson with words that invite the Spirit.
Pray about a person you want to strengthen. Share a gospel message and your testimony with that person.

blocks.text: Keep the review short. Let two or three learners share, and thank each one.
Welcome the class warmly. Begin with a prayer and a short thought from scripture to invite the Holy Ghost.
What happened when you tried last lesson’s invitation? Who would like to share?
Listen for: real experiences, effort made, one thing learned.
Try saying: “Before we start, who would like to tell us what happened when they tried last week’s invitation?”
Read the introduction aloud slowly. Then ask one learner to say it again in their own words.

parts.title: How the Spirit helps teachers and learners

blocks.text: Give each pair one reference. Share the findings aloud.

parts.title: Inviting the Spirit as you teach

blocks.text: Let each group show their skill in thirty seconds.

Four skills help: begin a lesson in a way that invites the Spirit, adjust your teaching to the needs of the person, teach for understanding, and listen. Let four groups each take one skill and say how it invites the Spirit.
How does keeping a message simple help the Spirit teach?
How does listening help?
Let learners write how they will use these skills.
Listen for: a good opening, fit to the person, simple message, careful listening.
Say: “Let’s begin with a prayer and a simple question.”
Model how to ask after a verse is read.

How can you tell when someone feels the Holy Ghost?

Read Doctrine and Covenants 11:12 in pairs.
Ask how it would help if someone asked what the Holy Ghost feels like.
Listen for: peace, warmth, clarity, a desire to do good.
Say: “Did you feel something different as we read? That feeling is the Spirit.”
Ask learners for one prompting they have followed.
